newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian CCB sees no repeat of H1 earnings jump.
newsitem.headline: Belgian CCB sees no repeat of H1 earnings jump.

text.p: Belgian publicly-owned bank Credit Communal de Belgique/Gemeentekrediet van Belgie (CCB) said on Wednesday second-half earnings should be good, but ruled out a repeat of the impressive first-half earnings growth.

"We will have a good second half, but it seems excluded that we would see a repeat of the 40 percent earnings growth of the first six months." chief executive officer Francois Narmon told a news conference.
He also said the strong 1996 half-year earnings growth was due to the fact that the year-earlier period, the first half of 1995, had been weak.

"In 1995 first-half profit was less than half of second-half profit, in 1996 we will see the opposite. The first half was excellent, the second half will probably be a lot less favourable," Narmon said.
Narmon also said that there would be no repeat of the write-back of provisions at CCB's 52-percent owned Luxembourg unit Banque Internationale a Luxembourg (BIL).
"Second-half provisions will increase slightly," he said.
CCB group's consolidated provisions fell 300 million francs to 5.25 billion in the first half, in contrast with other Belgian banks where provisions had to be increased.
Generale Bank on Tuesday reported that depreciation, write-downs and provisions rose to 13.30 billion in the first half, from 9.70 billion in the first half of 1995.

Narmon denied that CCB had made a special effort to book strong first-half earnings growth ahead of the planned partial bourse-listing of is shares in November, an operation which is part of its planned alliance with French bank Credit Local de France.
"People will think we did this (the profit jump) on purpose ahead of the bourse listing. That is not true, but it suits us well," he said.

Asked why BIL had not waited with the write backs so as to smooth out the volatility of the bank's earnings, Narmon said: "Now that we are ready to merge with CLF it was especially important that our balance sheet adequately reflect reality."
"We wanted to give potential investors a clear view of the situation. We did not want to manipulate the figures," he added.
CCB is Belgium's second-biggest bank, after Generale Bank.
-- Geert De Clercq, Brussels Newsroom +32 2 287 6813, Fax +32 2 230 7710
